scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
Hi — I'm Marcus, one of the senior research analysts here at Summit Point. Dana told me you'd be starting today, and I'm glad to have the help.

Here's the situation: new business is pouring in. Several companies have sent us **requests for proposals (RFPs)** — documents describing a business problem and asking us to propose the research that will solve it. Your first job is to read two of those RFPs and recommend the research methodology that best fits each client's objectives and budget.

Start with the **Inbox** on the left — I've forwarded you the RFPs from **SwiftCart** and **TrailTonic** along with some pointers. When you're ready, open each *Methodology Selection* assignment and make your recommendation. And don't skip the **Guides** button in the bottom right: it summarizes when each research method earns its keep.

inbox.subject: Welcome aboard!
inbox.body:
Welcome to Summit Point Research Group! I'm Dana Whitfield, the research director, and you'll be working on my team as a research analyst.

A quick word on how we operate: clients bring us decisions, not questions. Our job is to work backward from the decision they need to make to the evidence that would actually change it — and only then pick a method. Analysts who skip that step end up running beautiful studies that answer the wrong question.

You'll start on proposal work with Marcus this week. He's the best proposal writer in the shop; learn everything you can from him. Once you've had some practice, I'll be handing you something bigger — a prospective client called **Neo Smart Living** that could become the largest engagement of the year.

Glad you're here.

— Dana

inbox.subject: How to read an RFP (before you pick a method)
inbox.body:
Before you open the two RFPs, here's the discipline I use:

1. **Find the decision.** Somewhere in the RFP is a decision the client has to make. Underline it.
2. **Classify the evidence.** Would that decision be settled by *numbers that project to a population* (quantitative) or by *depth, language, and reasons* (qualitative)? Or by facts that already exist somewhere (secondary)?
3. **Check the constraints.** Budget, timeline, and deliverable expectations rule out methods that might otherwise fit.

Each methodology option in the assignment lists its description, deliverable, geographies, sample size, and interactions — read those details, they matter. A method can be *directionally* right but scoped wrong for the client.

Recommend exactly one methodology per client. I'll review both proposals and send you my feedback after you run the simulation.

— Marcus

inbox.subject: SwiftCart, Inc. RFP
inbox.body:
First client. SwiftCart runs same-day grocery delivery in eight metro areas and is deciding whether to expand into **same-day pharmacy delivery**. Their RFP is attached — read it closely before you choose.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — SwiftCart, Inc.
attachments.body:
**SwiftCart, Inc. — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** SwiftCart operates same-day grocery delivery in eight U.S. metropolitan areas, fulfilling roughly 40,000 orders per week through a network of gig shoppers.

**Business decision.** Leadership must decide by next quarter whether to enter same-day *pharmacy* delivery, and if so, how to position against incumbents.

**Research objectives.** We are seeking a research partner to help us understand:

- The current landscape of the same-day pharmacy delivery market
- Who the leading competitors are, and their approximate market shares
- Growth trends and forecasts for the category over the next five years
- Regulatory and partnership models used by existing players

**Constraints.** We need findings within **6 weeks** and have budgeted **$15,000–$20,000** for this phase. We expect a summary report with recommendations; primary data collection is *not* expected at this stage.

**Contact.** R. Okafor, VP Strategy, SwiftCart, Inc.

inbox.subject: TrailTonic, Inc. RFP
inbox.body:
Second client. TrailTonic sells functional beverages (electrolyte + adaptogen blends) through outdoor retailers and DTC. They want to know where their brand actually stands with the target market. RFP attached.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — TrailTonic, Inc.
attachments.body:
**TrailTonic, Inc. — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** TrailTonic manufactures functional beverages for outdoor athletes, sold through 900 specialty retailers and a direct-to-consumer site. After three years of growth, marketing spend is up for annual review.

**Business decision.** The board must allocate next year's marketing budget across brand-building versus performance channels. That allocation hinges on where the brand stands today.

**Research objectives.** We want to measure, among U.S. adults who exercise outdoors at least weekly:

- **Aided and unaided awareness** of TrailTonic versus competitors
- **Brand perceptions** on attributes such as taste, efficacy, and value
- **Purchase incidence and intent** for the category and for our brand
- Differences in the above across age groups and regions

Results must be **projectable to the target population** — we will present them to the board, so measurement precision matters more than depth of explanation.

**Constraints.** Findings needed within **8 weeks**; budget **$30,000–$40,000**.

**Contact.** J. Meade, CMO, TrailTonic, Inc.

guides.title: Rounds 1 & 2 — Choosing a Research Methodology
guides.body:
**Work backward from the client's decision.** Ask: what kind of evidence settles it?

| Method | Typically the right tool when… |
|---|---|
| Secondary research | The facts already exist: market size, competitor landscape, trends, benchmarks |
| Survey | You must *measure* attitudes or behavior and project results to a population |
| Focus groups | You need ideas, language, and reactions — new products, concepts, brainstorming |
| In-depth interviews | Respondents are experts, executives, or the topic is complex/sensitive |
| Observational research | You need actual behavior (not self-reports): shopping paths, decision moments, layouts |
| Mystery shopping | You're auditing whether protocols and service standards are followed |
| Experiment | You must isolate *cause*: does the new thing outperform the current thing? |

**Then apply the constraints.**

- *Quant vs. qual:* Words like **measure**, **projectable**, **precision**, and **how many** point quantitative. Words like **why**, **explore**, **ideas**, and **reactions** point qualitative.
- *Budget & timeline:* A method that fits the question but blows the budget or calendar is still the wrong recommendation.
- *One method rarely does everything.* In these first rounds, each client's RFP is best served by a single methodology — pick the one aimed at their **primary** objective, not a side interest.
